The network-wide mechanism links Canton Coin demand directly to synchronizer usage. Traffic payments remove coins through burns, connecting the token's role in network payments to the activity handled by production synchronizers.

data.title: Don't Lose Sleep Over GLP-1s. This Stock Is Still a Bargain. — Barrons.com
Mphasis, Coforge shine in strong Q2 for IT midcaps while Sonata faces seasonal headwinds
data.description:
New Delhi, Nov. 7 -- Mphasis Ltd capped a strong outing in the second quarter for India's mid-sized tech services companies, which were undeterred by an uncertain demand environment and cautious client spending.

However, the exception was Sonata Software, which reported revenue of $256 million on Friday, a 26% drop from the previous quarter. The second quarter is seasonally weak for Sonata's domestic business, which primarily involves selling software licences and makes up about three-fifths of the company's overall revenue. Fewer software licences are sold during the quarter.

A day earlier, Blackstone-owned Mphasis reported its best second quarter in five years with a 3.2% sequential increase in revenue to $486 million in the July-September period. Almost three-fourths of its incremental revenue came from financial institutions, which account for more than half of the company's overall business.

The two companies capped the earnings season for India's mid-sized tech services firms with annual revenues of $1 billion to $4 billion. Coforge Ltd was the fastest-growing tech services firm in Q2 while Hexaware Technologies Ltd was the slowest.

The two companies capped the earnings season for India's mid-sized tech services firms with annual revenues of $1 billion to $4 billion. Coforge Ltd was the fastest-growing tech services firm in Q2 while Hexaware Technologies Ltd was the slowest.

In terms of revenue growth, Coforge reported a 10.1% increase to $652 million in Q2, followed by Persistent Systems Ltd (up 7.8% to $488 million), Firstsource Solutions Ltd (up 2.8% to $296 million) and Hexaware Technologies (up 1.6% to $412 million).

Coforge and Firstsource Solutions reported their best second-quarter performance in two years, while Persistent Systems, the ninth-largest tech services company, reported its best second-quarter performance in five years.

This contrasts with the country's Big Six-Tata Consultancy Services Ltd, Infosys Ltd, HCL Technologies Ltd, Wipro Ltd, Tech Mahindra Ltd, and LTM Ltd-which did not post revenue growth of more than 2% from the preceding quarter. Wipro, the fourth largest, was the only one among the top 12 to report a sequential revenue decline in the quarter.

However, the Big Six had the upper hand in terms of profitability, save for Infosys, the second-largest IT company, whose operating margin fell 10 basis points, and TCS, whose margin remained unchanged. Each of the other four tech services companies widened their operating margins by up to 130 basis points.

Among the midcaps, operating margins remained unchanged at Coforge (16%) and Mphasis (14.8%) while they fell 100 basis points to 15% for Persistent Systems and 140 basis points to 12.2% for Hexaware Technologies. Sonata Software's margin jumped 180 basis points to 7.3%, and Firstsource Solutions' margin rose 10 basis points to 12.5%.

"Hexaware's growth has been lower than management's expectations in YTD-CY26 due to delay and/or reduction in spending in vendor consolidation deals and leadership changes at client's end," ICICI Securities analysts Ruchi Mukhija, Aditi Patil and Seema Nayak said in a note dated 30 October.

According to Vikas Swami, an equity research associate at InCred Equities, Coforge would have to ensure deal uptake to maintain growth.

"The strong order book reflects management's proactive focus on large deals and provides healthy revenue visibility. However, sustaining $1bn+ quarterly order intake remains key to maintaining the current growth trajectory," Swami said.

Coforge increased its full-year margin guidance by 50 basis points to 16% even as the rise of AI increases price wars among peers.

"This improvement in margin, at a time when our industry faces acute pricing pressure, is driven by our execution ethos," Sudhir Singh, chief executive officer (CEO) of Coforge, said during a post-earnings conference call on 23 October. "AI is breaking the link between scale and margin leadership for the tech services industry. Time and material, effort-based economics face pressure as automation reduces labor content."

The sector has faced uncertain demand due to geopolitical tensions in West Asia and the spectre of artificial intelligence, which threatens to eat into the work done by the country's largest IT services firms.

The uncertainty was reflected in the first-half report card of the midcaps, even though they had a promising second quarter. In the first six months of the fiscal, the midcaps grew in a range of 2% to 37% compared with 6% to 40% growth in the first six months of the preceding fiscal. However, this was better than their larger peers, which grew 0.5-6.5% in the first half.

For now, the mid-cap tech companies are not disturbed by this lingering demand uncertainty.

"We now expect revenue growth in the low double-digits range for the full year," Nitin Rakesh, chief executive officer of Mphasis, said during the post-earnings analyst call on 6 November. "Last quarter, our guidance was high single digit to low double digits. We are doing so despite an uncertain macro environment because it rests on results already delivered and on visibility we can see in the pipeline and the backlog."

Still, shareholders were not convinced. Shares of three of the midcaps closed lower a day after they announced their earnings. Shares of Persistent, Hexaware and Firstsource fell 1.7%, 5.9%, and 4.4% a day after they announced their September quarter earnings. Coforge was the outlier as its shares jumped 4.9%.

On Friday, Mphasis and Sonata Software shares closed 0.6% and 0.9% lower on the BSE.

data.title: A Cheap Play on the Aluminum Market — Barrons.com
data.description:
Alcoa may not be what it once was, but there's plenty of upside for investors.

By Andrew Bary

Alcoa offers an inexpensive play on an underappreciated commodity.

Alcoa may not be what it once was — a global industrial behemoth that was a member of the Dow Jones Industrial Average for more than 50 years, until 2013. But there is plenty of appeal for investors in a smaller Alcoa following the spinoff of its aluminum products business in 2016.

Here's why. Alcoa is the leading North American-based aluminum company. It has major operations in Australia, Brazil, and Canada, and a smaller footprint in the U.S., where it operates two of the country's four remaining aluminum smelters.

Alcoa has a presence in all stages of aluminum production. That involves the mining of bauxite, the purification of that ore into the intermediate compound of alumina, and the smelting of alumina to make aluminum using an electricity-intensive process. That method was developed by Alcoa in the late-19th century and remains little changed today.

The company's prospects are promising.

Alcoa produces about 3% of the world's aluminum, and is poised to increase its output by more than 30% to more than three million metric tons annually. That's thanks to its $4 billion purchase of AliGroup, a division of Australia's South32, which is due to close by the middle of 2027.

Alcoa's volatile shares look appealing. At around $38, they are trading just above their 52-week low, and for less than half their high of $85 in June. Alcoa trades for just six times projected 2026 earnings of $6.81 a share and seven times estimated 2027 profits of $5.50 a share.

That's low relative to mining peers, which generally fetch over 10 times earnings, and a third the S&P 500 multiple. Plus, the company produced ample free cash flow of about $600 million in the first nine months of 2026.

"Alcoa is a best-in-class integrated producer in an attractive commodity," says Steve Galbraith, managing member of Kindred Capital in Darien, Conn. He says the stock price drop since June is excessive, given that aluminum prices are down about 15% from their June high to $3,100 per metric ton, or $1.40 a pound. That means that Alcoa remains solidly profitable, given production costs of about $2,500 per ton.

"There has been no major downgrade in earnings estimates," Galbraith adds, "no crazy decline in the forward curve for aluminum prices and [global production] capacity has been relatively restrained." He believes the stock has upside of 50% from here.

In the metals space, copper has generated more excitement than aluminum because of tight market conditions, limited new supply, and electrification demand. The case for aluminum also looks good.

"There is growing demand driven by a number of megatrends like electrification and the energy transition, and strong packaging demand. Supply is constrained," Alcoa CEO William Oplinger told Barron's in an interview.

The metal's combination of strength and low weight make it ideal for aerospace, transportation, packaging, and other uses.

So, why is Alcoa trading so cheaply? Several reasons.

Investors are taking a wait-and-see approach to its AliGroup acquisition. Oplinger sees strong strategic and financial merit to the deal, which Alcoa unveiled at midyear. Integration and execution will be important. Alcoa is financing the deal mostly with debt, which will add some leverage to a balance sheet that is much improved over the past few years. Alcoa had just $1 billion of net debt before the coming transaction.

Wall Street reviews have been good so far. Jefferies analyst Chris LaFemina wrote in a recent client note that he sees "a path to a simpler and better Alcoa that we believe isn't fully reflected in the Alcoa share price."

Barclays analyst Richard Garchitorena recently initiated coverage of Alcoa with an Overweight rating and $55 price target, calling it a "crouching tiger, hidden dragon." His view: Lower aluminum prices are factored into the shares — and the AliGroup deal was smart, and is a potential 2027 catalyst due in part to $900 million in total projected synergies including logistics, technology improvements, and some cost reductions.

Another plus for investors: Alcoa's small market value of $10 billion, solid industry position, and scarcity value could make it a takeover candidate in the consolidating mining industry, although the company may have created a poison pill with the AliGroup deal.

One worry for investors: Aluminum prices spiked after the start of the Iran war, as Middle East production was curtailed. An end to the conflict could be a negative because of potentially higher output in the region, pressuring prices.

Tariffs are also an issue for Alcoa because Canadian aluminum — including sizable production from Alcoa's Quebec facilities — are subject to a 50% U.S. tariff. But for Alcoa, the tariffs are offset by high U.S. aluminum prices to the world benchmark. That is a reflection of scant domestic production relative to demand.

Aluminum demand is expected to exceed production this year, but some on Wall Street are concerned that supply could top demand in the coming years due to new production from Indonesia.

There's also the China factor. China accounts for about 60% of annual aluminum production and a similar amount of demand. China has imposed a cap on aluminum production to prevent oversupply, but its adherence to that cap is a risk, as is Chinese demand.

Nonetheless, global aluminum demand is expected to grow by 2% or so annually over the next decade, and by 3% in North America, a key Alcoa market.

CEO Oplinger says there are no pure-play Western companies with Alcoa's size in the aluminum market. "If someone wants to invest in the aluminum value chain, there's one choice: Alcoa."

Alcoa also is one of the better investments in the mining industry.
